papers.title: Distinct cortical functional network alterations in internet gaming disorder and alcohol use disorder: A resting-state EEG graph theory analysis.
papers.abstract: Internet gaming disorder (IGD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD) are characterized by compulsive behaviors and impaired impulse control. Although IGD is classified as a behavioral addiction and AUD as a substance use disorder, previous studies have suggested potential neurophysiological similarities between the two conditions. However, the frequency-specific topological organization of cortical networks in IGD and AUD remains poorly understood. This study compared the cortical functional networks in IGD and AUD using resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) and graph theory-based network analysis. A total of 151 subjects (49 patients with IGD, 48 with AUD, and 54 healthy controls (HCs)) participated in this study. Resting-state EEG data were preprocessed, followed by source reconstruction and network analysis. We examined global and nodal network characteristics across different frequency bands. At the global network level, IGD exhibited a significantly higher clustering coefficient (CC) and strength (weighted degree) in the beta frequency band compared to AUD and HCs. At the nodal level, the IGD group displayed significantly increased beta-band CCs and strengths in multiple brain regions, particularly the parietal and limbic areas. Notably, beta-band nodal CC and strength in the bilateral superior frontal gyri were significantly lower in AUD than in IGD. Beta-band nodal CC and strength measures showed nominal associations with AUDIT or IAT scores. Our findings suggest that IGD and AUD exhibit distinct cortical network patterns. The results provide further neurophysiological evidence distinguishing IGD, as an example of behavioral addiction, from alcohol-related substance addiction.

papers.title: Automated extraction of seizures and ictal-interictal continuum patterns from EEG reports to enable large-scale neurophysiology and neurocritical care research.
papers.abstract: Critical clinical information in EEG reports is often locked in free text, limiting large-scale research. This work develops and validates an automated, cross-institutional pipeline to extract seizures, rhythmic patterns, and ictal-interictal continuum features for population-level neurophysiology studies. We developed a five-stage hybrid pipeline comprising: (1) text normalization, (2) rule-based pattern filtering to focus the analysis on relevant report segments, (3) segment-focused prompt generation, (4) large language model (LLM) inference for structured attribute extraction, and (5) post-processing. This hybrid design combines the consistency of rule-based screening with the flexibility of LLM-based extraction from variable free-text EEG reports. The pipeline was applied to 156,582 EEG reports from three health systems (two adult, one pediatric). Performance was evaluated using a balanced set of 1,500 expert-reviewed samples, which extracted seizure presence, count, burden, and timing, as well as the frequency and prevalence of periodic and rhythmic patterns. Patterns included lateralized periodic discharges (LPD), generalized periodic discharges (GPD), and generalized/lateralized rhythmic delta activity (GRDA/LRDA). The pipeline achieved high performance across health systems for seizure (average accuracy 0.94) and periodic and rhythmic pattern detection (LPD: 0.97 [95 % CI: 0.94-0.99], GPD: 0.96 [0.92-0.98], GRDA/LRDA: 0.97 [0.94-0.99]). Seizure specificity was 0.72 at two adult institutions (95 % CI: 0.66-0.77) and 0.99 at the other two (one adult and one pediatric). Frequency and prevalence extraction showed strong agreement with mean values 0.94 and 0.93, respectively. High-frequency discharges (≥2 Hz) were associated with higher seizure occurrence within 24 and 48 h in descriptive analysis. This study introduces a scalable method for EEG analysis using clinical narratives, linking rhythmic patterns to seizure progression and supporting critical care risk stratification and large-scale EEG outcome prediction research.

papers.title: Microstate-specific functional connectivity in alcohol use disorder using resting-state EEG.
papers.abstract: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is often described as a "disconnection syndrome", reflecting neural dysfunction associated with chronic alcohol use. However, previous studies on functional connectivity of resting-state EEG (rsEEG) in AUD have reported inconsistent findings, possibly due to overlooking the brain's dynamic nature. We examined rsEEG in 26 young adults with AUD and 35 healthy controls (HC), using microstate analysis to characterise transient brain states and to estimate functional connectivity within each state. Although microstate map topologies were comparable between the two groups, the temporal dynamics of the AUD group were biased towards microstates C and D. Particularly within microstate C, the AUD group showed significantly greater functional connectivity across most frontal-occipital channel pairs, whereas significantly reduced functional connectivity was observed in the interhemispheric channel pairs. Moreover, compared with conventional functional connectivity estimates, microstate-specific functional connectivity yielded superior classification performance in distinguishing the two groups. In addition, the AUD group showed less stable hub-like properties in microstate C, indicating diminished network efficiency. Our findings suggest that transient EEG properties, exemplified by microstate-specific functional connectivity, provide informative neural markers for characterising the impact of alcohol use on the brain.

papers.title: Toward Closed-Loop Cognitive Modulation in Alzheimer's Disease: BCI-Relevant Evidence and a Translational Roadmap.
papers.abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) has entered a biomarker-defined era, yet most cognitive and neuromodulatory interventions continue to use fixed targets, timing, and doses. This targeted narrative review maps brain-computer interface (BCI) and closed-loop-relevant evidence in AD and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) by examining how sensing, control, and intervention modules are used prospectively. Read modules include electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), functional ultrasound (fUS) and transcranial ultrasound localization microscopy (t-ULM), and digital measures. Control functions include feature extraction, within-person state decoding, uncertainty-aware decision rules, target-engagement assessment, and safety oversight. Write modules include neurofeedback, sensory gamma and sleep-phase acoustic stimulation, transcranial alternating-current stimulation (tACS), transcranial direct-current stimulation (tDCS), repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), transcranial pulse stimulation (TPS), transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS), transcranial photobiomodulation (tPBM), and focused ultrasound-mediated blood-brain barrier (FUS-BBB) opening. Human studies have separately demonstrated signal-contingent feedback, individualized targeting, physiological target engagement, home delivery, and emerging sensing, while preclinical studies provide mechanistic support for gamma, optical, and ultrasound approaches. Sleep-phase acoustic stimulation additionally demonstrates early automated signal-to-stimulus control. Passive sensing provides observations, personalization sets baseline parameters, state-informed control uses current signals to alter delivery, and target engagement verifies the proximal response without establishing clinical efficacy. Reliable decoding of waking cognitive states, broader controller utility, and durable clinical benefit remain unvalidated. We therefore organize the field around disease context, state sensing, feature extraction, state decoding, bounded decision/intervention, response verification, and safety oversight. The decisive early design compares assignments to an adaptive policy with otherwise matched fixed delivery; a sham arm can additionally test intervention efficacy. Such trials must prespecify decoder calibration, uncertainty, abstention, safety limits, and mechanistic and clinical endpoints. Closed-loop cognitive modulation therefore defines a translational research agenda for AD.

papers.title: Platform Differences in Smartphone Sensing Features for Mental Health Across Four Annual College Cohorts: Secondary Analysis.
papers.abstract: Passive sensing for mobile mental health relies on observations that can differ across smartphone platforms. Distinguishing behavioral differences from differences in observation is necessary before using these features for symptom screening or monitoring. We quantified platform-associated differences, feature availability, sensitivity to preprocessing, and the predictive contribution of connectivity features within the Generalization of Longitudinal Behavior Modeling (GLOBEM) dataset and its collection and processing pipeline. We analyzed 4 annual US college cohorts from 2018 to 2021, comprising 705 annual records from 497 people reported by the dataset investigators. The feature sample contained 554 iOS and 151 Android records. Without verified cross-year identity links, inference and cross-validation were performed separately within each cohort. We compared 15 raw constructs and matched transformations using Cliff δ, participant resampling, and fixed logistic regression. Phone-derived location and screen features were separated from Fitbit activity and sleep measures. Analyses included coverage, complete cases, psychological adjustment, and retrospective depressive-symptom screening using the preceding 14 days. Total Bluetooth scan counts were lower on iOS in every cohort (Cliff δ -1.00 to -0.85). Connectivity counts differed more between platforms than core phone behavioral features did (difference in mean absolute Cliff δ 0.22-0.43; all 95% CIs above zero). Smaller observed-value differences did not imply equal coverage: 41 of 103 iOS records lacked all home-time values in 2020, compared with 0 of 34 Android records. Platform-classification area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.94 to 0.997 for 13 raw constructs, 0.34 to 0.91 after normalization, and 0.65 to 0.80 after discretization. Bluetooth differences persisted after psychological adjustment. In 661 eligible screening windows, behavioral-model AUROC ranged from 0.41 to 0.56. All behavioral, connectivity-added, and platform-added models had worse Brier scores than the intercept-only benchmark. Adding connectivity changed AUROC by 0.004 to 0.034; every paired 95% CI included zero. Within GLOBEM, selected connectivity features showed larger platform-associated differences than core phone behavioral features, while availability problems also affected location. Weak screening performance limits what these comparisons can establish about downstream harm. Platform-specific coverage and outcome calibration require assessment before interpreting sensing features as clinical markers.

papers.title: Frequency-Specific Thalamocortical Network Dynamics During Focal Seizures in Humans.
papers.abstract: The thalamus is an emerging neuromodulation target in drug-resistant focal epilepsy because of its frequent ictal involvement. However, frequency-specific and directional thalamocortical dynamics remain poorly understood. We sought to characterize thalamocortical network dynamics across seizure evolution using stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG). We retrospectively analyzed SEEG recordings from patients with pediatric-onset drug-resistant focal epilepsy with simultaneous cortical and thalamic sampling focusing on the anterior nucleus (AN) and centromedian nucleus (CM). We applied visual analysis with quantitative measures of spectral power, imaginary coherence, and spectral Granger causality across slow (1-12 Hz), β (13-30 Hz), and γ (30-70 Hz) bands to quantify thalamocortical and cortico-cortical interactions from seizure onset to termination. Random forest models were trained to classify seizure state using thalamic EEG features as an exploratory analysis. The final cohort comprised 19 patients (median age, 16.9 years; 31.6% female), with 66 focal seizures analyzed. Thalamic ictal activity was present at seizure onset in 81% of sampled thalamic contacts and became nearly universal by seizure termination. Both the thalamus and seizure onset zone showed increased spectral power during seizures, with prominent slow-band augmentation at seizure termination in the thalamus. Similarly, thalamocortical imaginary coherence increased during seizures, with the largest changes near seizure termination in the slow band (AN-SOZ: 11% [IQR, 2 to 20], rank-biserial correlations (rrb) = 0.84; CM-SOZ: 12% [IQR, 3 to 23], rrb = 0.84) and β band (AN-SOZ: 5% [IQR, 0 to 12], rrb = 0.74; CM-SOZ: 8% [IQR, 2 to 15], rrb = 0.86). Directed connectivity analyses demonstrated bidirectional thalamocortical interactions, with large slow-frequency thalamus-to-SOZ outflow near seizure termination from both AN and CM, exceeding propagation-zone-to-SOZ cortico-cortical flow (both p < 0.01). Seizure state was classified using thalamic EEG features, with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve values of 0.825 for AN and 0.839 for CM. Human focal seizures engage frequency-specific and bidirectional thalamocortical interactions that evolve from onset to termination. These findings support the thalamus as a source of clinically relevant seizure-state information and may inform thalamic biomarker development for neuromodulation in drug-resistant epilepsy.

papers.title: Identification of Type 1 and Type 2 α-Synuclein-Seeds by CSF Seed Amplification Assay in Patients With Movement Disorders.
papers.abstract: A novel α-synuclein (syn) seed amplification assay (synSAA) differentiates 2 types of syn-seeds in CSF: type1, associated with Lewy bodies (LBs), and type2, associated with glial-cytoplasmic inclusions, the hallmark of multiple system atrophy (MSA). However, syn-copathology extends beyond synucleinopathies, and copathologies are increasingly relevant. Different syn-seeds have been assessed in highly characterized research cohorts, but data assessing type and frequency in patients from routine clinical encounters are lacking. Hence, our objective was to determine frequency, type, and clinical association of different syn-seeds in CSF in a large cohort from a movement disorders (MDs) clinic. This cross-sectional study included consecutive patients from a MD clinic between 2009 and 2025. CSF was tested with synSAA and clinical data derived from medical records. We recruited 1,059 patients (mean age 70.5 ± 10.5 years; 38.4% female; mean disease duration 4.0 ± 4.6 years). Syn-seeds were detected in 54.2% of patients, with type1-seeds predominating (88.5%). High synSAA positivity was observed in Parkinson disease (PD) (84.7%), dementia with LB (93.4%), MSA (84.5%), isolated REM-sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) (80.0%), and normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) with PD (87.0%). Undetermined hypokinetic MD showed 53.7% positivity. Moderate proportions (∼25-33%) were detected in Alzheimer disease, progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal syndrome, and idiopathic NPH without PD, while other neurologic disorders showed 20.9% positivity. Type2-seeds were the major seed type in MSA (79.6% of syn-seeds) and minor type in PD (6.2%), PSP (9.1%), and undetermined hypokinetic MD (13.8%). Overall, type2-seeds were present in only 2.6% of non-MSA patients. Patients with type1-seeds had worse olfaction and more hallucinations. Multivariable regression identified impaired olfaction (OR = 0.67 per point increase of identified smells out of 12, higher scores indicating better olfaction) significantly associated with type1-seeds. Our results provide reference data on syn-seed frequency in routine clinical patients, demonstrating that type1-seeds indicate common underlying syn-pathology or copathology associated with hyposmia and hallucinations. Type2-seeds are specific to MSA and detection of type2-seeds outside the clinical MSA spectrum can improve diagnosis of patients with atypical presentations because our results match neuropathologic MSA studies. In vivo identification of different seed types will improve diagnosis, clinical trial stratification, and development of targeted therapies.

papers.title: Deciphering the impact of chronological age on sleep stage transition dynamics for disorder classification.
papers.abstract: Ageing and sleep disorders are closely linked, as physiological changes can increase sleep fragmentation in older adults. Although sleep stage transition probability (STP) features provide useful markers of sleep disruption, age-related variability presents challenges for generalised sleep disorder classification. This study investigated the influence of chronological age on sleep disorder detectability and compared age-agnostic, age-involved, and age-specific machine learning (ML) approaches. Using single-night hypnograms across three data groups, two-stage STP features were extracted and evaluated through five experimental configurations, including models without age information, models incorporating age as a feature, and models stratified by age group. Statistical validation using absolute differences between transition probability matrices was performed to assess healthy-disordered differences across age cohorts and thresholds. Age-involved models provided modest improvements of approximately 2-4% in accuracy and F1-score over age-agnostic models, which achieved approximately 85% performance. Age-specific modelling demonstrated greater benefits, particularly among older subjects (age≥60), with improvements of approximately 8-12%. Older cohorts generally achieved 12-18% higher performance than younger cohorts, with XGBoost and other ensemble models producing the strongest results. In contrast, younger age-specific models showed lower or more variable performance, suggesting reduced discriminability of two-stage STP features. Statistical analysis identified more pronounced healthy-disordered differences in NREM transitions involving N2 and N3 among older subjects. Age-threshold analysis indicated that discriminability increased from the 50s and was strongest around 55-60 years. These findings suggest that chronological age influences the diagnostic relevance of hypnogram-derived transition features and that age-specific modelling may offer advantages for sleep disorder screening, particularly in older adults. However, independent external and prospective validation remains necessary before clinical implementation.

papers.title: Innovative mHealth intervention providing sustained anticipatory guidance (zero cavity): Design, validation, user perception and effectiveness - A randomized controlled trial protocol.
papers.abstract: Early Childhood Caries (ECC) remains one of the most common chronic conditions in childhood, affecting over 600 million children globally. When untreated, it can lead to severe pain, abscesses, difficulty in chewing that contributes to malnutrition, impaired speech, disrupted sleep, low self-esteem, social withdrawal, and poor academic performance, all of which diminish a child's overall quality of life. Although largely preventable, ECC remains highly prevalent because of delayed preventive care and low parental awareness. Effective health education needs to be consistent, accessible, and available whenever parents need it. Although current evidence indicates that anticipatory guidance is a proven approach, its long-term reinforcement through a mobile app has not yet been tested. This study aims to develop and evaluate the effectiveness of a mobile health (mHealth) application delivering Sustained Anticipatory Guidance (SAG) for the prevention of ECC. A two-arm parallel hospital-based randomized controlled trial will be conducted at Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education & Research, Chennai, India. The study will enrol 540 mother-infant dyads from the departments of Pediatric Medicine and the Centre for Early Childhood Caries Research (CECCRe). Eligible dyads with infants aged 6-12 months in the predentate stage will be randomized to the "Zero-Cavity" mHealth app (intervention) or standard care (control). Baseline and semi-annual data on oral hygiene, fluoride exposure, and feeding/diet will be collected. Calibrated dentists will perform quarterly clinical exams using ICDAS II criteria, recording cavitated and non-cavitated lesions. For children at high risk or with enamel defects/incipient lesions, clinical photographs will be taken to support individualized preventive guidance. The primary outcome will be the effectiveness of the app in preventing ECC, while the secondary outcomes will include ECC incidence and prevalence. Despite being largely preventable, ECC remains a major public health challenge, sustained by limited preventive access and inconsistent counselling, especially in LMICs. This trial evaluates the Zero Cavity app, believed to bridge this gap by providing sustained, age-appropriate anticipatory guidance beyond clinic settings on oral development, hygiene, diet/feeding, and fluoride use. The behavioural theory-driven approach is expected to enhance cultural relevance, usability, and behaviour change, with optimism that process evaluation will illuminate engagement and implementation. It is believed that this large, adequately powered, parallel-group RCT with intention-to-treat analysis will offer, with optimism, a scalable, low-cost model that will expand the reach and consistency of continuous preventive care in diverse urban and peri-urban populations. CTRI/2026/04/107305. Trial access: https://ctri.nic.in/Clinicaltrials/pmaindet2.php?EncHid=MTQyNDEw.

papers.title: Sleep quality patterns and associated factors in patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis: A latent class analysis.
papers.abstract: Sleep disorders are highly prevalent among patients undergoing maintenance hemodialysis (MHD) and significantly affect their physical and mental health. However, sleep quality is inherently multidimensional, and previous studies have largely adopted binary classifications to distinguish good from poor sleep quality, which may obscure heterogeneous sleep patterns in this population. The study aimed to identify distinct sleep quality patterns using latent class analysis and to explore factors associated with each pattern. A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted among 667 MHD patients from seven hospitals in eastern China between June 2022 and May 2024. Participants' sociodemographic and disease-related data were collected via structured questionnaires; sleep quality, depressive symptoms, and anxiety symptoms were assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, the Patient Health Questionnaire-9, and the Generalized Anxiety Disorder-7, respectively. Latent class analysis based on the seven components of the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index identified three distinct sleep quality classes: "good overall sleep quality" (Class 1, 52.8%), "insomnia with daytime dysfunction" (Class 2, 36.7%), and "poor overall sleep quality with low sleep efficiency" (Class 3, 10.5%). Using Class 1 as the reference, multinomial logistic regression showed that older age, anxiety symptoms, and depressive symptoms were positively associated with Class 2; older age, smoking, and depressive symptoms were positively associated with Class 3, whereas higher personal monthly income (> 2000 China Yuan) was negatively associated with Class 3. Prolonged dialysis vintage (≥ 15 years) was strongly associated with Class 2 and Class 3, yet these associations were sensitive to the cutoff value for dialysis vintage and disappeared when a 10-year threshold was applied. Overall, these findings may help inform targeted sleep assessment, particularly for older patients, smokers, and individuals with anxiety or depressive symptoms.

papers.title: Noninvasive inference of presymptomatic abiotic stress in Solanum Lycopersicum from latent electrophysiological dynamics via action potential-based model.
papers.abstract: Early detection of abiotic stress in Solanum lycopersicum is critical for yield protection, yet current methods rely on visible symptoms that manifest only after irreversible physiological damage. Plant action potentials (APs), which directly reflect ion channel activity across the plasma membrane, represent an underexplored avenue for presymptomatic, noninvasive stress detection. We hypothesized that stress-induced alterations in ion channel activity would produce measurable changes in AP waveform morphology before visible symptoms appeared. One hundred sixty S. lycopersicum cv. Moneymaker plants, spanning two prospectively defined cohorts (80 for classifier development, 80 for detection-window quantification), were assigned to control, salinity (100 mM NaCl), osmotic (PEG-6000, -0.4 MPa), or K⁺/N deficiency groups. APs were recorded noninvasively using a Plant SpikerBox, and five physiologically interpretable parameters were extracted via phenomenological curve fitting. Two models were evaluated: logistic regression (LR) on biophysical parameters and a convolutional neural network (CNN) on raw waveforms. Assessed on a single locked held-out partition of 39 recording sessions shared by both models, LR did not underperform the CNN (accuracy 0.923 vs. 0.897; ROC-AUC 0.955 vs. 0.976). The paired difference in ROC-AUC was not distinguishable from zero (ΔAUC = -0.022, 95% CI -0.106 to +0.041), and confidence intervals are wide and overlapping at this sample size; the comparison should be read as a failure to detect a difference rather than as a demonstration of equivalence. Applied prospectively to an independent cohort, the classifier detected stress 5.25 ± 2.96 days before visible symptom onset across all three stress conditions, with all individual presymptomatic detection windows positive, while issuing no sustained positive call on any concurrently recorded control plant. This work establishes individual tomato plant action potentials as quantitative probes of physiological state, with direct implications for precision agriculture.

papers.title: Prospective associations between prolonged sleep onset latency and the co-development of sleep disturbances and mental health problems among preschoolers: a population-based longitudinal study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and mental health problems frequently co-occur in childhood, but their symptom-level dynamics during early development remain unclear. Prolonged sleep onset latency (SOL) may be sensitive to changes in both domains during the preschool years, when expanding psychosocial demands and structured routines may challenge sleep initiation. We examined longitudinal symptom-level associations between sleep disturbances and mental health problems to identify potential symptoms with prominent prospective links, particularly prolonged SOL, that may inform symptom-specific early prevention strategies. Data came from a three-wave cohort of children aged 3-6 years recruited from 191 preschools in Shanghai, China. Parent-reported sleep disturbances and mental health problems were assessed using the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ) and the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ). Cross-lagged panel network models examined longitudinal symptom-level associations. Prolonged SOL was assessed using frequency-based and duration-based measures from the CSHQ sleep onset delay item and parent-reported SOL duration (>20 min), and examined in relation to subsequent mental health problems using logistic regression. Among 16,575 children (mean [SD] age, 3.73 [.29] years; 51.9% boys), co-occurring sleep disturbances and mental health problems were 9.6%, 7.0%, and 6.1% from wave1 to wave3. Sleep-onset-delay showed high out-expected influence in both adjacent-wave networks (.30 and .34), indicating prominent prospective associations with subsequent symptoms of sleep disturbances and mental health problems. Frequency-based prolonged SOL was associated with overall mental health problems at both subsequent waves (AORs = 1.32-1.33, both ps < .001), while duration-based prolonged SOL (>20 min) was consistently associated with subsequent hyperactivity (AORs = 1.26-1.28, both ps < .001). Prolonged SOL showed prominent prospective associations within the co-development of sleep disturbances and mental health problems and may serve as an early signal and potential intervention target for promoting sleep and mental health in preschool children.
papers.journal: Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines

papers.title: Component specific sleep-cognition associations in ICU professionals in India.
papers.abstract: Rotating shift work in intensive care units (ICUs) disrupts circadian alignment and sleep homeostasis, impairing cognition. Global sleep and cognitive scores may obscure component- and domain-specific effects, and testing multiple sleep components against multiple cognitive domains risks false-positive findings unless corrected. To examine associations between individual Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) components and item-level Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) performance in ICU healthcare workers, with multiple-comparison correction and adjustment for confounders. Cross-sectional study in a tertiary hospital in eastern India. Forty-five ICU professionals working rotating shifts completed the PSQI (seven components, scored continuously) and MoCA (eight item scores plus one derived composite). Spearman correlations were computed for all 63 pairs, with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction within each PSQI-component family. Associations reaching nominal significance were tested in multivariable linear regression adjusted for age, sex, occupation and ICU experience, with robust standard errors and bootstrap confidence intervals. Five of 63 correlations reached nominal significance (P < 0.05). Only daytime dysfunction with the attention-executive composite survived both correction and adjustment (rho = -0.43, corrected P = 0.026; adjusted beta = -0.94, 95% CI -1.50 to -0.38, P < 0.001; adjusted R-squared = 0.31). Sleep latency with digit span and sleep medication use with trail making persisted after adjustment but not after correction. Only daytime dysfunction was associated with cognitive performance, specifically attention-executive performance, after both correction for multiple testing and adjustment for confounders, supporting a targeted rather than global approach to sleep-related cognitive risk in critical care.

papers.title: Agent Orange Exposure and Diagnosis of Parkinson Disease and Related Disorders Among US Veterans.
papers.abstract: The risk of Parkinson disease (PD) due to Agent Orange, the Vietnam War Era defoliant, is inferred from studies of agricultural pesticide exposure. Epidemiological work is currently lacking. To examine the association between Agent Orange exposure with incident cases of synucleinopathies including Parkinson disease, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) among US veterans. This was an electronic health record-based cohort study inclusive of medical records from January 1, 1999, to December 30, 2022. Veterans were followed up for a mean (SD) of 12.5 (7.0) years from the start of records. Analyses were conducted from July 2024 to July 2026. The setting was the US Department of Veterans Affairs and included US veterans who served during the Vietnam War Era (August 1964 to May 1975) were screened. Those with incomplete demographic data or prevalent synucleinopathies before or within 6 months of follow-up were excluded. Agent Orange defined by self-report. Direct or occupational exposure was defined by involvement in Operation Ranch Hand, Army Chemical Corps, and/or direct handling or spraying. Cumulative incidence of synucleinopathies was calculated adjusting for competing risk of death, age, traumatic brain injury, and frailty. After screening of 4 917 272 US veterans, 4 468 509 veterans (mean [SD] age, 60.6 [8] years; 4 380 139 male [98%]) were included in analyses. A total of 1 035 210 veterans (23.2%) had Agent Orange exposure; 7600 (0.2%) of these had direct or occupational exposure. Birth year, age at time 0 (start of records), sex, race, ethnicity, and smoking history were balanced among the exposed and unexposed groups with further adjustment for traumatic brain injury and frailty. Agent Orange exposure was associated with higher risk of PD (hazard ratio [HR], 1.44; 95% CI, 1.37-1.52), RBD (HR, 1.78; 95% CI, 1.68-1.89), and DLB (HR, 1.66; 95% CI, 1.32-2.09). Associations strengthened when enriched for direct or occupational exposure, including PD (HR, 1.99; 95% CI, 1.71-2.32) and RBD (HR, 2.25; 95% CI, 1.87-2.70). Results were robust to additional adjustment for traumatic brain injury, frailty, health care utilization, and multiple imputation. Sensitivity analyses indicated that substantial unmeasured confounding would be required to explain the observed associations. Results of this cohort study suggest that Agent Orange may be an independent risk factor for later development of PD and related conditions. This finding has implications for global policy change. Further studies are needed to understand the mechanism underlying this association, gene-toxin interactions, and whether there is a unique clinical phenotype to those exposed to Agent Orange.

papers.title: Reduced Social Media Use and Change in Internalizing Symptoms Among High-Risk Young Adults.
papers.abstract: National cohort analyses of the association between reduced social media use and subsequent improvement in internalizing problems among high-risk young adults-ie, those most likely to benefit from intervention-remain limited. To assess whether reduced social media use is associated with improvements in internalizing problems among US young adults with frequent social media use and elevated internalizing problems. This cohort study used data from the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health Study (2013-2021). Repeated observations were organized into 4 consecutive, overlapping 3-wave intervals, each comprising 3 sequential survey waves (t, t + 1, and t + 2); for example, interval 1 included waves 1-3, and interval 4 included waves 4-6. Young adults aged 18 to 24 years with elevated internalizing problems (all 4 symptoms) and frequent social media use (several times a day) at wave t were included. Data were analyzed from February to August 2026. Self-reported social media use frequency at wave t + 1 (nonfrequent [≤once daily] vs frequent [several times daily]). Past-year internalizing problems (nonelevated [≤3 symptoms] vs elevated [4 symptoms]) at wave t + 2 via the Global Appraisal of Individual Needs-Short Screener (depression, anxiety, psychological distress, sleep difficulties). A total of 3788 person-interval observations (2561 [64.7%] female; aged 18-24 years at baseline) were included. Approximately 14% (n = 540) transitioned to nonfrequent use at t + 1. Reduced use was associated with greater likelihood of nonelevated internalizing symptoms at t + 2 (0.57 vs 0.49; prevalence difference, 0.07; 95% CI, 0.02-0.13; prevalence ratio, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.04-1.27). Findings were generally consistent across sensitivity analyses, including alternative exposure definitions (weekly or less vs several times daily social media use: prevalence ratio, 1.17; 95% CI, 1.04-1.33), alternative missing-data handling approaches (prevalence ratio, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.04-1.25), design-based analyses (prevalence ratio, 1.16; 95% CI, 1.06-1.28), concurrent models (prevalence ratio, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.01-1.26), and alternative outcome definitions using internalizing symptom counts, with non-frequent use associated with fewer symptoms (adjusted incidence rate ratio, 0.90; 95% CI, 0.85-0.96). In this cohort study, reduced social media use was associated with subsequent improvement in internalizing symptoms among US young adults with elevated symptoms and frequent use. These findings identify reduced social media use as a potentially modifiable target for prevention and early intervention in this high-risk population.

papers.title: Investigating Modified Deep Learning Models for Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder Classification Using Electroencephalography Spectrograms.
papers.abstract: This study developed neurophysiologically informed data augmentation strategies to improve electroencephalogram (EEG)-based deep learning classification of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children with limited labeled EEG data. ADHD affects approximately 8.0% of children and adolescents worldwide, or about 129 million individuals aged 5-19 years. Clinical diagnosis relies largely on behavioral observations; EEG provides objective biomarkers, but conventional image augmentation may not preserve disease-relevant neural oscillation patterns. We introduced band-shuffle augmentation, which exchanges selected spectral content between samples within the same diagnostic class at the level of canonical EEG frequency bands. The method was evaluated through systematic architecture optimization, augmentation experiments, and integration into an adaptive multistrategy training pipeline. Band-shuffle augmentation achieved 75.05% validation accuracy, 75.76% F1 score, 75.30% sensitivity, and 74.56% specificity, exceeding the 74.32% accuracy of traditional computer vision augmentation. The integrated multistrategy framework achieved 77.47% validation accuracy and 0.8414 AUC, improving accuracy by 27.0% over the 60.99% MobileNetV2 baseline and by 4.2% over conventional augmentation. The results support frequency band-level augmentation as a neurophysiologically informed approach to EEG spectrogram classification. Ablation indicated distinct module contributions, and Grad-CAM highlighted frequency-specific regions consistent with ADHD neurophysiology. This framework may support EEG-based computer-aided screening, although external validation is required before clinical use.

papers.title: Neurophysiological and Sleep-Related Effects of a Cosmetic Shampoo and Conditioner Regimen in Adults with Scalp Discomfort: A Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: Scalp discomfort is prevalent and associated with impaired quality of life and sleep disturbance. Although pruritus is linked to neurophysiological alterations and sleep disruption, these effects of cosmetic scalp care remain unexplored. This pilot study evaluated the neurophysiological and sleep-related effects of a cosmetic shampoo and conditioner regimen in adults with scalp discomfort and mild sleep disturbances. This observational pilot study enrolled 21 adults with scalp discomfort and sleep difficulties, of whom 20 were analyzed. After 1 baseline week and 1 washout week, participants used the cosmetic shampoo and conditioner at least three times weekly for 2 weeks. Neurophysiological outcomes were assessed with electroencephalography (EEG; arousal, valence, sleepiness, and anger levels) at baseline, post-washout, week 3, and week 4. Sleep was evaluated with the Stanford Sleepiness Scale, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, Insomnia Severity Index, and Fitbit Inspire 2 tracking. Scalp discomfort was assessed with a clinical report form. Data were analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. During the second reflective question set (Q2), EEG analysis showed significant improvements in mood valence (p < 0.001) and sleepiness (p = 0.021); arousal and anger levels did not change significantly. All four validated sleep questionnaires improved significantly: morning sleepiness decreased by 11.9% (p = 0.011) and overall sleep difficulty by 23.5% (p < 0.001) at week 3 and daytime sleepiness by 30.7% (p < 0.001) and insomnia severity by 35.9% (p < 0.001) at week 4. In an exploratory post hoc subgroup with below-average baseline deep sleep (n = 9), wearable tracking showed a 20.6% increase in deep sleep duration (p = 0.016); no significant change was observed in the full sample. Scalp itch intensity decreased by 49.1% (p < 0.001) and weekly discomfort days by 40.6% (p < 0.001). In this single-arm pilot study, use of the regimen was associated with improved scalp discomfort and with neurophysiological and sleep-related changes. Combining EEG, wearable tracking, and validated sleep instruments may offer a more objective framework for evaluating cosmetic scalp care. The deep sleep finding is hypothesis generating only. This study was retrospectively registered on 25 June 2026 on ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT07680608.

papers.title: Correction: Circadian rhythms and sleep disturbances: a conceptual perspective with implications for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.
Dynamic functional reversibility versus static anatomical burden: a multidimensional prediction model for velopharyngeal surgery outcomes in OSA.
papers.abstract: Conventional static anatomical assessments inadequately predict velopharyngeal surgery outcomes in obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). This study aimed to develop and validate a prediction model integrating awake structural burden, sleep-state morphology, and pharmacological reversibility. In this prospective cohort study, 106 consecutive OSA patients (modeling cohort) underwent velopharyngeal surgery following standardized evaluation including the TCM score, polysomnography, and drug-induced sleep endoscopy (DISE) with dexmedetomidine. Dynamic reversibility was quantified by the proportional change in apnea-hypopnea index following nasopharyngeal tube insertion (ΔAHI-DISE) and oropharyngeal lateral wall collapse patterns. An independent cohort (n = 28) served for temporal validation. Multivariable logistic regression was used to construct a nomogram, with performance assessed by discrimination (AUC), calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test, Brier score), and decision curve analysis. Static anatomical metrics (TCM score) showed modest discrimination (AUC 0.667, 95%CI 0.568-0.765). Dynamic parameters demonstrated superior predictive value: ΔAHI-DISE achieved an AUC of 0.769 (95%CI 0.674-0.864), and oropharyngeal lateral wall response to nasopharyngeal tube insertion remained independently predictive (odds ratio 0.254, 95%CI 0.089-0.688, P = 0.008). The integrated nomogram (TCM + dynamic metrics) achieved robust discrimination (AUC 0.822, 95%CI 0.740-0.904), significantly outperforming TCM alone (DeLong test, Z = 3.42, P < 0.001). Calibration was excellent (intercept 0.000, slope 1.000, Brier score 0.167). Temporal validation showed acceptable discrimination (AUC 0.728, 95% CI 0.535-0.921) but limited calibration (slope 0.524, intercept 0.112), indicating a need for recalibration rather than confirmed transportability; the optimal cutoff shifted from 0.545 to 0.697 in the lower-BMI validation cohort. Dynamic functional reversibility may outperform static anatomical burden in predicting velopharyngeal surgery success. The proposed nomogram may provide preliminary individualized risk stratification, but prospective multicenter validation and recalibration remain warranted.

papers.title: Comparison of thyromental angle, scalloped tongue, and dental arch dimensions across obstructive sleep apnea severities in a Thai patient group: a cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: This cross-sectional study sought to compare dental arch dimensions, intraoral features, and soft-tissue markers among obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) severity subgroups in Thai patients. Adult patients (N = 103) with polysomnography-confirmed OSA diagnoses were stratified according to apnea-hypopnea index score. Dental arch dimensions were obtained from three-dimensional digital models. Intraoral examinations included overjet, overbite, scalloped tongue, and oral tori. Soft-tissue facial profile, mandibular projection, thyromental angle (TMA), and thyromental distance were assessed using standardized photographs. Demographic data, polysomnographic parameters, and Thai Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores were recorded. Continuous variables were compared using one-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis H-tests, categorical variables assessed with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests, respectively, with post hoc testing as appropriate. Statistical significance was set at p-value < 0.05. Adjusted analyses were performed using ANCOVA or ordinal regression, depending on the type of variable. The patients were categorized into mild, moderate, and severe OSA groups. Lower nadir oxygen saturation (p < 0.001) and higher Thai version of the Epworth Sleepiness Scale scores (p = 0.002) were observed in the severe OSA group. Overjet, overbite, and most dental arch dimensions showed no significant difference. TMA increased with severity (p < 0.001). After adjustment for covariates, the findings for TMA and scalloped tongue remained significant. No significant difference was found in thyromental distance, facial profile, mandibular projection, or torus prevalence. Most craniofacial and intraoral features showed no statistically significant difference across OSA severity levels, whereas differences in TMA and scalloped tongue were observed across severity groups, highlighting the multifactorial nature of OSA and the need for comprehensive clinical assessment.

papers.title: Effects of housing system on locomotor activity and circadian rhythmicity in llamas (Lama glama).
papers.abstract: Precision Livestock Farming technologies provide objective tools to assess animal behavior and welfare under different management conditions, yet their application to South American camelids remains limited. This study evaluated the effects of housing system on locomotor activity and circadian rhythmicity in adult llamas (Lama glama) using accelerometer-derived data. Ten llamas (2 males, 8 females) were monitored during two consecutive phases: a grazing-confinement system, in which animals grazed during the day and were housed at night, and a continuous housing system without access to pasture. Locomotor activity was recorded continuously using neck-mounted triaxial accelerometers, and circadian rhythms were assessed using a 24-h cosinor model. Mean locomotor activity was significantly lower (P < 0.001) during continuous housing compared with the grazing-confinement phase, with reductions of approximately 33% in males and 47% in females. In both sexes and housing systems, locomotor activity exhibited a clear diurnal pattern, with higher activity during the light phase than during the dark phase (P < 0.001). Cosinor analysis revealed significant circadian rhythms with a stable 24-h periodicity and acrophases clustered in the early afternoon. While acrophase timing was not affected by housing system, continuous housing significantly reduced MESOR, amplitude, rhythm robustness, and circadianity indices (P < 0.001). These findings demonstrate that spatial restriction and loss of pasture access constrain locomotor behavior and weaken the temporal organization of activity in llamas, while the persistence of circadian rhythmicity suggests a preserved endogenous timing system. The integration of accelerometry and circadian analysis provides a valuable approach for objective welfare assessment in camelid production systems.

papers.title: Knockdown of KCNQ2 in CA1 reshapes epilepsy-related limbic network rhythms and reduces spontaneous exploratory behavior in mice.
papers.abstract: Circuit-level effects of localized cornu ammonis 1 (CA1) potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily Q member 2 (KCNQ2) loss-of-function on epileptogenesis remain poorly understood, despite the well-established association of KCNQ2 deficiency with epilepsy and neuropsychiatric comorbidities. To examine how CA1-specific KCNQ2 deficiency modulates neural network activity during acquired epileptogenesis, we selectively knocked down KCNQ2 in mouse CA1 via adeno-associated virus (AAV)-short hairpin RNA (shRNA) and explored limbic network alterations. Calcium activity of glutamatergic neurons, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) ergic neurons, somatostatin-positive (SST+) interneurons, and parvalbumin-positive (PV+) interneurons was recorded using cell type-specific GCaMP expression with simultaneous CA1 electroencephalography (EEG). Multi-site EEG recordings from CA1, cornu ammonis 3 (CA3), retrosplenial agranular cortex (RSA), infralimbic cortex (IL), cingulate cortex area 1 (CG1), primary motor cortex (M1), and basolateral amygdala (BLA) were analyzed for spectral power, functional connectivity (FC), and phase-amplitude coupling (PAC). We observed spontaneous activity, novel object recognition, and social behaviors of the model mice. CA1 KCNQ2 knockdown increased calcium activity in all neuronal populations during the latency, with greater activation of SST+ than PV+ interneurons. Excitatory-inhibitory imbalance correlated with seizure severity. EEG analyses revealed a biphasic pattern: reduced low-frequency power, phase synchrony, and FC during the latency, followed by widespread hypersynchronization of power spectral density, mutual information, and phase synchrony during severe seizures. In the non-epileptic state, PAC analysis revealed that knockdown group developed a biased network configuration characterized by enhanced PAC directed toward the BLA and weakened CA3-M1 and M1-related coupling. This pattern was consistent with their behavioral phenotypes, including reduced central exploration, fewer open-arm entries, impaired novel object exploration, and decreased social preference. During generalized seizures, PAC underwent extensive reorganization, with strengthened coupling between the BLA and multiple brain regions and reduced M1-directed coupling. Intraperitoneally administered retigabine (RTG), a pan-KCNQ channel opener, partially alleviated these behavioral deficits and attenuated the abnormally potentiated long-range network activity. CA1 KCNQ2 knockdown not only disrupts the local excitatory/inhibitory balance but also promotes epileptogenesis by reshaping limbic-cortical network coupling patterns.

papers.title: Invasive monitoring and mapping in epilepsy surgery: Acute and chronic intracranial recording from surface to depth.
papers.abstract: Invasive intracranial recording remains central to the surgical evaluation of drug-resistant focal epilepsy when noninvasive data are insufficient to define the epileptogenic zone or its relationship to eloquent cortex. This review, part of an International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) Surgical Therapies Commission education series aligned with the epilepsy surgery curriculum, reviews invasive monitoring and mapping for the practicing and trainee epilepsy surgeon. Consistent with the competency-based ILAE epilepsy surgery curriculum, in which the surgeon is expected to understand and actively contribute to electrode selection, safe implantation, and the interpretation of invasive recordings within the multidisciplinary team, we give particular emphasis to the surgical execution of these methods alongside their electrophysiological rationale. We outline the historical development of the field from intraoperative electrocorticography and subdural recording to stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG), describe acute and chronic recording strategies using both surface and depth approaches, including the operative techniques of implantation and post-implantation electrode localization, and summarize the techniques of functional mapping. We compare subdural and stereotactic methods with respect to coverage, mapping capability, diagnostic yield, seizure outcome, and morbidity, and we review the complication profiles of each. Finally, we discuss future directions, including high-density and chronically implantable probes that combine macro-contacts with microelectrode recording throughout the electrode shaft. We emphasize that the choice of method should follow a clearly stated anatomo-electro-clinical hypothesis, balancing the completeness of sampling against procedural risk.
authors: Tatiana V H F de Oliveira
