papers.title: Ideal sleep duration as a potential explanation of the bimodal chronotype: An exploratory study.
papers.abstract: Regarding circadian typology, the existence of a fourth category, the bimodal types, was previously proposed. Bimodal types would be those answering some questions as morning types, while others as evening types, resulting in a different sleep-wake cycle compared to intermediate types. The aim of this study was to further explore the plausibility of this new circadian typology category, attempting to determine whether it qualifies as a genuinely new category of individuals or merely a byproduct of another individual difference, namely ideal sleep duration. To this end, we reanalyzed data previously collected from 1583 children and adolescents (817 females, mean age of 13.13 ± 1.96) and 2115 adults (1144 females, mean age of 44.50 ± 5.64) who completed the Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire for Children and Adolescents (MEQ-CA) and the MEQ, respectively. The open-ended questions on the ideal bedtime and get-up time were used to compute the ideal total sleep time that was later grouped into three categories: short- (≤6 hours), medium- (6 < x < 12 hours), and long sleepers (≥12 hours). In children and adolescents, bimodal types were overrepresented in both short and long sleepers and underrepresented among medium sleepers; separately considering the gender variable, the same pattern of results was detected in males only. Regarding adults, an overrepresentation of bimodal types was observed among long sleepers and their underrepresentation among medium sleepers; this same distribution was replicated only in males. It seems that the suggested fourth category of circadian typology, that of bimodal types, may be considered as a byproduct of the individual difference in ideal sleep duration.

papers.title: Climate change anxiety and insomnia in nursing students: implications for health promotion?
papers.abstract: Climate change is not only an environmental crisis but also an emerging mental health concern. This study investigated the relationship between climate change anxiety and insomnia severity among nursing students in the Mediterranean Region of Turkey. A descriptive cross-sectional survey was conducted with 512 participants between December 2024 and January 2025. Data were collected using the Descriptive Information Form, the Climate Change Anxiety Scale (CCAS), and the Insomnia Severity Index (ISI). The mean CCAS score was 1.63 ± 0.69 and the mean ISI score was 13.20 ± 4.18. Correlation analysis revealed a moderate positive relationship between climate change anxiety and insomnia severity (r = 0.372, p < 0.001). Regression analysis indicated that climate change anxiety was a significant predictor of insomnia severity, accounting for 13.9% of the variance. Insomnia severity was also associated with demographic factors such as short or long sleep duration, smoking, chronic mental disorders, and screen exposure. Climate change anxiety is associated with increased insomnia severity among nursing students, highlighting the mental health implications of climate-related psychological stress. Health promotion initiatives within universities should incorporate resilience-building, sleep hygiene education, and mental health support to address climate-related anxiety. Further longitudinal and multicenter studies are warranted to confirm these findings and guide effective public health interventions.

papers.title: First Seizure Services: Status and Healthcare Professional Attitudes and Perspectives. Results From a Survey of the European Academy of Neurology.
papers.abstract: Dedicated first seizure services (FSSs) may improve the early assessment, diagnosis, and management of people presenting with a suspected first seizure, but little is known regarding their current status in Europe. In this study, we aimed to explore the availability of FSSs throughout Europe, as well as to investigate attitudes towards their implementation among healthcare professionals involved in epilepsy care. We designed a web-based survey that was distributed through the European Academy of Neurology. The survey assessed respondent characteristics, local FSS availability, service organization, perceived utility, and barriers to implementation. A total of 441 participants from 72 countries completed the survey; 379 unique centers were included in center-specific analyses. Overall, 171/331 centers in geographical Europe (51.7%) reported an available FSS. Availability varied significantly by region, being highest in Northern Europe (74.0%) and lowest in Eastern Europe (35.5%). FSS availability correlated positively with Gross Domestic Product and current health expenditure per capita of the respondent's country. Participants reported a positive attitude towards FSSs: 90.9% believed that they should be a standard of care, 93.2% believed they improve outcomes, and 83.0% believed that they are cost-effective. The main reported barriers to implementation were limited infrastructure, financial constraints, organizational barriers, and a shortage of specialized personnel. FSS availability across Europe remains heterogeneous, with substantial variation according to geographical area and a possible association with economic factors. Despite implementation barriers, healthcare professionals expressed overall positive support for standardized first seizure pathways.

papers.title: Diet and Sex Influence Central Amygdala Neuroimmune Regulation of Binge Behaviors.
papers.abstract: Central amygdala (CeA) neuroimmune signaling is thought to play a critical role in binge behavior toward ethanol (EtOH) and high-fat diet (HFD), but the specific mechanisms by which CeA neuroimmune activity regulates binge intake, and how this system may be impacted by diet and sex, remain unclear. To test this, we assessed intermittent HFD/limited-access EtOH (iHFD + EtOH) intake with chemogenetic Gi-DREADD modulation of CeA astrocytes timed either immediately before drinking sessions or during HFD access in male mice. We then assessed CeA astrocytic Ca2+ dynamics and whole-cell electrophysiology of CeA glutamatergic transmission. We further compared impacts of two lab maintenance "chow" diets (Teklad 8604 vs. Bio-Serv F4031) on iHFD + EtOH intake in males and females and preliminarily assessed changes to two major CeA neuroimmune signals. Gi-DREADD actuation in CeA astrocytes immediately prior to drinking sessions selectively reduced EtOH intake, suggesting CeA astrocytes provide session-proximal control over EtOH behaviors. Gi-DREADD actuation in CeA astrocytes during iHFD access periods did not reduce HFD or EtOH intake. Prior iHFD + EtOH history sensitized CeA astrocyte Ca2+ responses to EtOH and elevated baseline and EtOH-evoked glutamatergic drive. Maintenance diets differentially impacted EtOH intake and modified CeA IL-10 and IL-13 levels, dependent on diet, sex, and binge history. Together, these data indicate that CeA astrocytes exert session-proximal control over binge-like EtOH intake, and diet/EtOH history sensitizes both CeA astrocyte signaling and CeA glutamate transmission. Critically, maintenance diets and sex may interact as modulators of drinking phenotypes and CeA neuroimmune signals. These findings identify CeA astrocytes as mechanistic entry points for interventions and establish diet and sex as essential experimental variables for studies of binge alcohol and palatable food intake.

papers.title: Synergistic electro-mechanical stimulation promotes neural stem cell differentiation in a 3D conductive and stretchable hydrogel.
papers.abstract: The limited understanding of how to physically manipulate neural stem cell (NSC) differentiation into mature neurons and functional glial cells in a three-dimensional (3D) environment has constrained the potential of NSC-based therapies for neurodegenerative diseases. In this study, we develop gelatin-methacryloyl (GelMA) and polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA)-based conductive hydrogels to investigate the effects of electrical stimulation (ES) and mechanical stretching on neuronal differentiation in a 3D matrix. GelMA and PEGDA provide extracellular matrix (ECM)-like biological and physical characteristics, enabling the study of neural differentiation, development, and electrophysiology. Poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene):polystyrene sulfonate (PEDOT:PSS) was incorporated into the GelMA/PEGDA matrix as a conductive additive to enhance hydrogel conductivity. Compared with non-conductive hydrogels, conductive hydrogels alone promoted neuronal differentiation, while conductive hydrogels combined with ES further enhanced neural differentiation, neurite extension, and neural gene expression. Mechanical stretching similarly induced neuronal differentiation and directional neurite alignment. Notably, co-stimulation with stretching and ES exerted synergistic effects, significantly promoting neurite outgrowth (2.5-fold compared to the unstimulated hydrogel control (GelMA-PEGDA)), increasing filopodia density by 15%, and enhancing neurite branching by 3%. Co-stimulation also upregulated neuronal differentiation marker expression, including for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), neuron-specific class III β-tubulin (Tuj-1), and microtubule-associated protein 2 (MAP2), and increased the neuronal electrical activity of encapsulated cells. Overall, this study advances the understanding of directed NSC differentiation within a 3D microenvironment using defined physical cues and provides a theoretical basis for improving the effectiveness and feasibility of NSC-based therapies.

papers.title: International Surgical Sleep Society Position Statement: Hypoglossal Nerve Stimulation for Obstructive Sleep Apnea in Adults.
papers.abstract: To review evidence regarding hypoglossal nerve stimulation (HNS) efficacy and adherence since regulatory approval over a decade ago. To understand predictive factors for surgical success with HNS and complication rates. Literature review and creation of International Surgical Sleep Society position statement based on available evidence. Literature review. A position statement working group was convened within the International Surgical Sleep Society (ISSS), including content experts from ISSS Committees. A literature search was undertaken, querying the PubMed, EMBASE, and Cochrane databases for studies reporting data on HNS for patients with OSA between 2010 and 2026. The results of the literature search were included in an ISSS position statement, which was sent electronically for approval by the ISSS Board of Directors. This manuscript utilized data from 43 studies to create a position statement on HNS as a therapeutic option for OSA. Data regarding efficacy and usage were summarized with surgical response ranging from 67% to 83% and adherence 5.6 to 7.7 h/night. Predictors of HNS success were examined, with mixed results related to body mass index, age, sex, and comorbid conditions such as insomnia. Complications after HNS, while low, should be discussed with patients prior to implantation. HNS is safe, effective, and should be considered part of a comprehensive approach to the management of OSA. The literature is currently mixed regarding predictors of HNS success. Future research to refine selection criteria for HNS will help sleep providers create a personalized approach to individual OSA phenotypes.
papers.journal: Otolaryngology--head and neck surgery : official journal of American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery

papers.title: [Guided orthodontic-surgical management of hyperdivergent skeletal class II malocclusion with obstructive sleep apnea: A case report].
papers.abstract: Unjustified premolar extractions, as well as extractions made necessary by severely compromised teeth, can complicate presurgical orthodontic preparation. Likewise, incomplete skeletal movements may result in surgically disappointing aesthetic outcomes while failing to address functional disorders such as obstructive sleep apnea. A complex case of skeletal class II malocclusion is presented, with a comprehensive analysis from initial diagnosis to treatment completion. The therapeutic stages included the orthodontist's diagnostic assessment, compared with that of the surgeon, the definition of shared objectives, and the joint implementation of a treatment plan involving orthodontic decompensation followed by guided surgery. The surgery was performed without intermediate splints and proved complex because of the choice and extent of the osteotomy procedures: counterclockwise rotation of the palatal plane and the mandibular corpus. The therapeutic alternatives, limited by the patient's initial dental situation and functional problems, are discussed. With regard to both diagnosis and overall orthodontic and surgical treatment, this case report allows the authors to share the method and resources they used to undertake this type of treatment with minimal risks.

papers.title: [Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea syndrome and myofunctional rehabilitation: A preliminary survey of French practitioners].
papers.abstract: Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (pOSA) affects 1-5% of children and may lead to significant neurocognitive, metabolic, and cardiovascular morbidity. Although adenotonsillectomy remains the first-line treatment, recent French guidelines recommend a multidisciplinary approach incorporating orthodontic treatments and orofacial myofunctional therapy (OMT). This preliminary national study aims to assess perceptions and practices related to OMT among different healthcare professionals in France. An 18-item online questionnaire was distributed between March and June 2025 to orthodontists, maxillofacial physiotherapists, and speech therapists. A total of 135 responses were analyzed. The most frequently reported dysfunctions were orofacial hypotonia (91%) and lingual motor immaturity (88%). Interprofessional differences were observed regarding proprioception, cervico-cephalic posture, short upper lip, and relative macroglossia. Physiotherapists emphasized nasal hygiene, whereas orthodontists focused more on orofacial habits and swallowing. Overweight was generally underestimated as an associated factor. The main barriers to OMT implementation included limited access to specialists, lack of training, insufficient interdisciplinary collaboration, and limited recognition of this approach. The observed variations may reflect differences in professional training, terminology, or sampling bias. These results, based on self-reported practices, do not allow assessment of the clinical effectiveness of OMT in pOSA. However, they confirm the high prevalence of dysfunctions in pOSA and highlight the need to develop a common language, strengthen care networks, and improve the integration of OMT in France.

papers.title: Daridorexant in treatment refractory cluster headache: A retrospective case series.
papers.abstract: Cluster headache (CH) is one of the most excruciating pain conditions known in humans. Most patients experience nocturnal attacks, which further worsen sleep quality and overall quality of life. The management of CH includes acute and preventive treatments, and in some cases, transitional therapy with corticosteroids may be used to achieve pain freedom in a shorter time while giving preventive therapy. We report our preliminary experience with daridorexant, a selective dual orexin receptor antagonist approved for chronic insomnia, as an adjunctive treatment in patients with treatment refractory CH, nocturnal attacks, and bad quality of sleep. Our objective was to describe within-patient changes in nocturnal attack frequency, sleep quality, and headache-related disability before and after add-on daridorexant in refractory CH. In this single-center, retrospective before-after case series, we reviewed clinical data from 10 patients followed at the Headache Center of the San Carlo Borromeo Hospital in Milan (Italy) between June 2023 and December 2024, with a diagnosis of either episodic or chronic CH, who experienced nocturnal attacks, sleep disturbances, and with inadequate response to standard treatments, including verapamil, lithium, or corticosteroids. In these patients, daridorexant was administered as add-on therapy, to treat the chronic insomnia. The frequency and features of CH attacks, sleep quality, headache-related disability, and quality-of-life evaluations were assessed before and after treatment. Treatment with daridorexant was associated with a significant reduction in nocturnal attacks, from 13.1 ± 7.5 to 6.4 ± 7.7 attacks per week (p < 0.050; n = 10/10). Patients also reported improved quality of life, with mean subjective quality-of-life scores increasing from 37% ± 15.6% to 61% ± 20.4% (p = 0.001; n = 10/10). Headache-related impact was reduced, with mean Headache Impact Test 6 scores decreasing from 62.0 ± 7.4 to 48.8 ± 16.2 (p < 0.050; n = 10/10). In addition, no patient reported worsening on the Patient Global Impression of Change scale, and eight of the nine out of 10 available Patient Global Impression of Change ratings indicated improvement. Daridorexant was generally well-tolerated, with adverse events reported in three out of 10 patients (30%), leading to treatment discontinuation in one patient. Daridorexant was significantly associated particularly with a reduction in the number of nocturnal attacks in patients with CH refractory to conventional therapies. These pilot preliminary results suggest a potential role for daridorexant as an adjunctive option for patients with CH, particularly those with a poor response to traditional therapies, nocturnal attacks, and sleep disturbances. Further prospective, controlled studies are warranted to confirm these findings and clarify the mechanisms underlying the observed clinical benefits.

papers.title: Perceptual Uncertainty Drives Serial Dependence in Facial Identity Across Multiple Perceptual and Memory Stages.
papers.abstract: Attractive serial dependence (SD) in facial identity is known to occur when stimulus judgments of a current face are drawn toward a face from the recent past. SD is thought to manifest at multiple levels of processing, including perception and working memory (WM). Whether SD facial identity effects emerging at different levels of processing reflect interacting perceptual and WM mechanisms remains unclear. In the present study, we used a facial matching task with varying perceptual uncertainty interspersed with a task with varying WM load to investigate the interactive contribution of perceptual and WM processing to SD in facial identity. Event-related potentials (ERPs) were analyzed to explore the neural mechanisms related to perceptual and WM processes underlying SD. SD increased with greater perceptual uncertainty but was not significantly affected by variations in WM load, and no interaction between the two was observed. However, ERP results showed that SD in facial identity emerged from multiple mechanisms involving both perception and WM. Altogether, perceptual uncertainty emerged as a primary driver of SD, modulating both early face-selective responses and downstream processes related to maintenance, retrieval, and monitoring.

papers.title: Comparing Fatigue Assessment Tools in Hemodialysis: Implications for Nephrology Practice From the Technology Assisted Stepped-Collaborative-Care Trial.
papers.abstract: Fatigue is a debilitating symptom experienced by patients treated with hemodialysis (HD). The standardized outcomes in nephrology-hemodialysis fatigue (SONG-HD-fatigue) and patient-reported outcome measurement information system (PROMIS-fatigue) instruments have not been used extensively among patients treated with HD. Our study evaluated the psychometric properties and treatment response of these measures compared to the commonly used functional assessment of chronic illness therapy-fatigue (FACIT-F) in HD. Technology assisted stepped-collaborative-care was a randomized controlled trial to evaluate the effectiveness of a stepped-collaborative-care intervention for symptom management in HD. Participants were adult patients receiving in-center 3-times-weekly maintenance HD at 14 dialysis units. We compared the performance of the SONG-HD-fatigue (3 items) and PROMIS-fatigue (7 items) against the FACIT-F (13 items) by evaluating their comparative psychometric performance (known-groups validity, convergent and divergent validity, screening utility, within-patient reliability, and responsiveness to treatment). Among participants (N =160; age 57.8 years, 35% female, 27% Black, and 15 % Hispanic), the median baseline FACIT-F score was 44. Patients experiencing higher baseline fatigue levels demonstrated significantly lower social support, physical function, physical activity, and sleep quality, and increased pain intensity, pain interference, depression, and anxiety. SONG-HD-fatigue and PROMIS-fatigue had similar direction and strength of correlations as FACIT-F with these outcomes. A SONG-HD-fatigue score of 4.5 and a PROMIS-fatigue score of 56.8 corresponded to a FACIT-F score of 30 for screening for clinically significant fatigue. The mean difference between the technology assisted stepped-collaborative-care intervention and control group at the 3-month primary outcome timepoint was significant for the PROMIS-fatigue and FACIT-F measures but not for the SONG-HD fatigue. Small sample size. SONG-HD-fatigue and PROMIS-fatigue had strong correlations with the validated FACIT-F questionnaire, suggesting that they can be helpful screening measures to identify patients treated with HD with significant fatigue. However, they were not as sensitive in capturing response to treatment.

papers.title: Orgasmic Meditation, Sleep, and Next-Day Somatic Distress: A 30-Day Observational Study.
papers.abstract: Orgasmic Meditation (OM) is a structured attention-training practice conducted between two people who follow a predefined set of detailed instructions. One person, the stroker, gently strokes the clitoris of the other person, the strokee, for 15 minutes while both place their attention on the point of contact and notice what they feel. Climax is not the goal. This study examined whether OM practice was associated with app-assessed sleep and next-morning Tumescence Survey responses. In this 30-day observational study, 41 experienced OM practitioners enrolled, and 36 contributed analyzable data, yielding 1,026 participant-nights. The Sleep Cycle Premium application assessed sleep quality, duration, regularity, and time to sleep onset. Each morning, participants reported whether they had practiced OM the previous day and completed the 15-item Tumescence Survey. Linear mixed-effects models accounted for repeated nights from the same participants and separated within-person from between-person associations. OM practice was not significantly associated with sleep quality (b = -1.87 index points; 95% CI: -3.96 to 0.21; p = .079), sleep duration (-10.11 minutes; 95% CI: -22.37 to 2.15; p = .106), time to sleep onset (+2.01 minutes; p = .225), or sleep regularity (+0.05; p = .948). On mornings after OM, participants reported less dissociation from their bodies and less agitation. These two item-level associations remained significant after correction for 15 comparisons. Craving and irritability scores were slightly lower after OM, but the differences were not statistically significant. Factor 2, which combined craving, physical discomfort, agitation, and dissociation, was lower after OM in the primary model (b = -0.77; 95% CI: -1.17 to -0.37; p < .001). The estimate weakened when the OM association was allowed to vary among participants (b = -0.67; 95% CI: -1.36 to 0.02; p = .056). Sleep did not mediate or modify this association. With OM practice and sleep duration in the same model, a day of OM was associated with the same reduction in Factor 2 as 3.8 additional hours of sleep (95% CI: 1.8 to 9.5), and with the same reduction in the total survey score as 1.7 additional hours (95% CI: 0.2 to 3.9). Climax was reported on 19.4% of OM days and was not associated with sleep outcomes within OM days. OM practice was not associated with app-assessed sleep in this sample. On mornings after OM, participants reported less dissociation from their bodies and less agitation, and these differences were not explained by sleep duration. The difference associated with an OM day was comparable in size to the difference associated with 3.8 additional hours of sleep for Factor 2 and 1.7 additional hours for the total survey score. The estimates weakened when the OM association was allowed to vary among participants. This comparison describes the relative size of observational associations and does not show that OM reduces sleep need. The sample was small and highly selected, and neither the sleep application nor the Tumescence Survey has been validated for this use. Controlled studies using validated measures are needed.

papers.title: Combined Associations of Maternal Sleep Quality and Prenatal Negative Life Events with Childhood Parasomnias.
papers.abstract: Parasomnias are common in early childhood and are increasingly linked to later behavioral and neurodevelopmental vulnerability. Although prenatal determinants of childhood parasomnias are recognized as an emerging research focus, evidence remains limited. Maternal sleep disturbances and psychological stress frequently co-occur during pregnancy and may have long-term implications for offspring health. This study examined the combined associations of maternal prenatal sleep quality and stress exposure with childhood parasomnias. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 6236 preschool-aged children, with maternal prenatal negative life events (NLEs) and sleep quality retrospectively assessed across three gestational periods. Childhood parasomnias were assessed using the Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire. Inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) was applied to reduce group differences across exposure groups. Associations were examined using logistic regressions, and path analysis was performed to estimate direct and indirect effects. Overall, 25.7% of children had parasomnias, with the highest prevalence in the co-exposure group (37.3%), followed by the poor-sleep-only (29.6%), NLEs-only (23.1%), and no-exposure groups (22.8%). After IPTW, maternal poor sleep quality during pregnancy was associated with increased odds of childhood parasomnias (aOR = 1.402, 95% CI: 1.231-1.596). While NLEs alone were not independently associated with parasomnias, co-exposure to poor sleep quality showed an even stronger risk (aOR = 1.778, 95% CI: 1.122-2.816). Associations appeared stronger among children whose mothers reported lower perceived family support. Path analysis revealed a direct association between maternal sleep quality and childhood parasomnias (β = 0.127, 95% CI: 0.083-0.172). Poor maternal sleep quality during pregnancy was directly associated with increased risk of childhood parasomnias, and co-occurring NLEs further amplified this risk. These findings highlight the importance of jointly assessing maternal sleep quality and psychosocial stress during pregnancy to identify children who are susceptible to developing parasomnias.

papers.title: Quillaic acid and echinocystic acid attenuate atherosclerosis: evidence from in vitro and in vivo studies.
papers.abstract: Atherosclerosis (AS) is an inflammatory disease characterized by the formation of lipid-laden lesions in arterial walls. Quillaic acid (QA) and echinocystic acid (EA) are natural pentacyclic triterpenes with diverse biological activities. However, whether QA and EA can ameliorate AS has not been reported. In this study, we first investigated the effects of QA and EA in reducing foam cell accumulation and inflammation in vitro. Then, the therapeutic effects of QA and EA (i.p., 5 mg/kg) were evaluated in ApoE knockout (ApoE-/-) mice fed a high-fat/high-cholesterol diet. In vitro experiments demonstrated that both QA and EA suppressed oxidized low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL)-induced foam cell formation by inhibiting cholesterol uptake and also inhibited lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced inflammatory responses. In high-fat/high-cholesterol diet-fed ApoE-/- mice, QA or EA treatment significantly reduced serum lipid levels, decreased inflammatory factor release, and attenuated atherosclerotic plaque formation. At the tested dose, EA showed slightly better anti-inflammatory and plaque-reducing effects than QA. Transcriptomic profiling revealed enrichment of genes associated with "Cell adhesion molecules" and immune response pathways in the aorta of QA-treated mice. For EA, enrichment was observed for genes involved in "Circadian rhythms" in both liver and aorta, as well as genes related to "Vascular smooth muscle contraction" and the "cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP)-protein kinase G (PKG) signaling pathway" in aortic tissues. Real-time quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis confirmed altered expression of selected circadian rhythm-related genes in the liver of EA- and QA-treated mice and in ox-LDL-induced foam cells. EA also increased cGMP levels in these foam cells. This study provides the first evidence for the anti-atherosclerotic effects of QA and EA and offers new insights into the potential of natural products for the treatment of cardiovascular diseases.

papers.title: Maniform Presentation of Behavioral Variant Frontotemporal Dementia Mimicking Late-Onset Mania: A Diagnostic Challenge.
papers.abstract: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a neurodegenerative disorder that may initially present with behavioral and affective symptoms, often mimicking primary psychiatric conditions, such as bipolar disorder, leading to frequent misdiagnosis. We report the case of a 70-year-old woman with no prior psychiatric history who presented with a first episode of maniform behavior, characterized by euphoria, disinhibition, decreased need for sleep, impulsive spending, and socially inappropriate conduct, mimicking late-onset bipolar disorder. Neuropsychological evaluation revealed significant executive dysfunction. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated bilateral frontal and anterior temporal lobe atrophy consistent with behavioral variant FTD (bvFTD). This case highlights the diagnostic challenge of distinguishing late-onset manic syndromes from neurodegenerative disease. It underscores the importance of integrating clinical history, cognitive assessment, and neuroimaging to improve diagnostic accuracy and avoid misdiagnosis.

papers.title: Neurophysiological changes following intensive Naikan therapy in a patient with recurrent depressive episodes later diagnosed with bipolar II disorder: A case report.
papers.abstract: Intensive Naikan therapy is a structured Japanese psychotherapy involving systematic reflection on interpersonal relationships; however, its neurophysiological correlates remain unclear. We herein report changes in resting-state electroencephalography (EEG), the P300 event-related potential, and standardized low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA)-estimated source activity after intensive Naikan therapy. A 29-year-old man with recurrent depressive episodes and anxiety about family relationships and future employment underwent 7 days of inpatient intensive Naikan therapy. He was later diagnosed with bipolar II disorder after a hypomanic episode during the follow-up. Assessments were performed before and after the intervention. Anxiety decreased on State-Trait Anxiety Inventory state and trait scores (42 to 20 and 30 to 20, respectively), and depressive symptoms remained minimal on the Hamilton Depression Rating Scale and Beck Depression Inventory (4 to 3 and 0 to 0, respectively). Psychological measures suggested reduced self- and other-blame and greater acceptance of family members. Resting-state EEG showed a negligible change in peak alpha-band global field power, whereas peak beta-band global field power decreased from 5.13 × 103 to 2.84 × 103 µV2/Hz. During the auditory oddball task, P300 amplitude at Pz increased from 5.5 to 7.3 µV. sLORETA images were evaluated descriptively, without statistical comparisons or uncertainty estimations. Intensive Naikan therapy was temporally associated with reduced resting-state beta activity and an increased P300 amplitude. These observations from a single uncontrolled case with multiple assessments are hypothesis-generating and do not establish treatment efficacy, causality, or a treatment mechanism.
papers.journal: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences

papers.title: Associations of Serum Gamma-Aminobutyric Acid and Docosahexaenoic Acid Levels with Pediatric Sleep Disorders: A Cross-Sectional Observational Study.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the serum levels of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) among children with sleep disorders, to generate preliminary hypotheses for future research. A total of 95 consecutively enrolled children newly diagnosed with sleep disorders from January to July 2024 were included in this cross-sectional observational study. Blood GABA and DHA levels were measured using API 4500 liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry system. Sleep disorders were classified by physicians according to ICSD-3 criteria based on structured parental interviews supplemented by brief sleep habit questions, without objective sleep monitoring such as polysomnography or actigraphy. No significant differences in GABA and DHA serum levels were found between genders. Within these children diagnosed with sleep disorders, significant inter-age differences in serum GABA and DHA were observed, younger patients exhibited higher serum GABA and DHA relative to older patients in the same clinical sample. Children with insomnia showed lower serum GABA than those with parasomnia (unadjusted for age confounding). A positive correlation between GABA levels and maternal education was observed. No significant difference in DHA was observed between insomnia and parasomnia. Maternal education was positively correlated with GABA in univariate analysis, but this association did not remain significant in multivariable models. Younger children with sleep disorders had higher GABA and DHA serum levels, and children with insomnia had lower GABA than those with parasomnia, whereas no significant difference in DHA was observed between these two groups. These cross-sectional correlational findings cannot establish causality. Definitive evaluation of serum GABA and DHA as candidate biomarkers requires further studies.

papers.title: Management of Recurrent Depressive Disorder, Anxiety, and Insomnia in a Patient With Philadelphia Chromosome-Positive Acute Lymphoblastic Leukaemia Receiving Dasatinib Therapy: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Psychiatric symptoms, including depression, anxiety, and insomnia, are common among patients with cancer and may complicate the management of oncological disease. This report presents a case of a patient with Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL) receiving dasatinib treatment who experienced a recurrence of depressive symptoms accompanied by insomnia, severe anxiety, and fatigue. The case highlights the challenges of psychopharmacological management in the context of potential drug-drug interactions associated with concomitant oncological treatment. A 55-year-old woman was admitted to a psychiatric inpatient unit because of worsening depressive symptoms, insomnia, severe anxiety, and fatigue. Pharmacological treatment was adjusted during hospitalisation, with treatment decisions influenced by potential pharmacokinetic interactions, QT interval prolongation risk, and the patient's concerns regarding medication changes. In addition to pharmacological treatment, the patient participated in a multidisciplinary psychiatric rehabilitation programme. During hospitalisation, her overall clinical condition gradually improved, with improvements in mood, anxiety, and sleep. Individualised psychopharmacological treatment, careful consideration of potential drug-drug interactions, and collaboration between psychiatrists and oncologists are important in the management of psychiatric comorbidity in patients with ALL. Patient engagement in treatment decisions may further support a treatment approach tailored to individual needs.

papers.title: The Effect of Nursing-Implemented Swaddling and Dim Light on Sleep Patterns and Weight Gain in Preterm Infants: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
papers.abstract: BackgroundPreterm infants admitted to neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) are highly vulnerable to sleep disruption caused by environmental stressors such as excessive light exposure, frequent handling, and routine caregiving procedures. Disturbed sleep may negatively affect neurodevelopment, physiological stability, and growth. Developmentally supportive nursing interventions, including swaddling and environmental light reduction, are intended to minimise sensory stress and support behavioural regulation. ObjectivesTo evaluate the association of nursing-implemented swaddling combined with dim light exposure with sleep patterns and short-term weight gain among preterm infants. DesignQuasi-experimental controlled study with repeated measurements. MethodsThe study was conducted on a purposive sample of 60 preterm infants allocated to an intervention group (n = 30) and a control group (n = 30). Infants in the intervention group received standardised swaddling and dim light exposure during designated rest periods in addition to routine NICU care, whereas the control group received routine care only. Sleep-wake behavioural organisation was assessed daily for five consecutive days using the Anderson Behavioral State Scoring System (ABSS), and body weight was measured daily using a calibrated electronic infant scale. Data were analysed using non-parametric statistical tests, including the Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon signed-rank, and Friedman tests. ResultsBaseline characteristics were comparable between groups for gestational age, birth weight, baseline weight, and APGAR scores; however, postnatal age was significantly higher in the intervention group (p = .004). Infants receiving swaddling and dim light demonstrated significantly greater improvements in sleep-wake behavioural organisation across the five-day study period than infants receiving routine care (all p < .001). The intervention group also showed significantly higher mean body weight at Day 5 (p = .009) and a higher mean discharge weight. ConclusionNursing-implemented swaddling combined with dim light exposure was associated with improved sleep-wake behavioural organisation and higher mean body weight at Day 5 and discharge among preterm infants, supporting the incorporation of developmentally supportive nursing practices into routine NICU care.

papers.title: Prevalence of suboptimal health status and its association with insomnia and smartphone addiction among medical students in Palestine: A multi-university cross-sectional study.
papers.abstract: Suboptimal health status (SHS) is a reversible intermediate state between health and disease. It is associated with the early development of chronic conditions and is strongly influenced by lifestyle factors. Medical training may foster unhealthy lifestyle patterns that increase long-term health risk. This study assessed the prevalence of SHS and the associations of insomnia and smartphone addiction with SHS among medical students in Palestine. A multi-university cross-sectional study was conducted among 461 medical students from five medical faculties in the West Bank, Palestine, between October 2025 and January 2026. Data were collected using a structured online questionnaire incorporating the 25-item Suboptimal Health Status Questionnaire (SHSQ-25), the Smartphone Addiction Scale-Short Version (SAS-SV), and the Athens Insomnia Scale (AIS). Group differences were examined using chi-square and independent t-tests, and binary logistic regression was performed to identify factors independently associated with SHS. Among 461 participants (mean age: 20.93 ± 2.02 years; 55.1% female), 47.5% were classified with SHS, 67.2% had smartphone addiction, and 65.5% reported insomnia. In multivariable logistic regression, insomnia showed the strongest association with SHS (AOR = 7.26, 95% CI: 4.26-12.39, p < 0.001), followed by smartphone addiction (AOR = 2.48, 95% CI: 1.47-4.20, p < 0.001). SHS was common among Palestinian medical students; insomnia and smartphone addiction were independently associated with SHS. These findings support the need for further longitudinal research and targeted sleep and digital health focused interventions to address SHS and promote student well-being.

papers.title: Slow-Wave Enhancement Reduces Axonal Injury in Murine Traumatic Brain Injury.
papers.abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is a major cause of death and disability as well as impaired cognition and sleep-wake abnormalities. The pathological hallmark of TBI is disturbed axonal transport and accumulation of proteins, leading to diffuse axonal injury (DAI). Recent studies suggest a role for slow-wave sleep (SWS) in the clearance of harmful extracellular proteins and functional recovery. Our group previously found that increasing SWS after TBI in rats improved cognition and decreased accumulation of injury-related histological markers in cortex and hippocampus, indicating a neuroprotective role of SWS. Though growing evidence suggests that sleep can improve the outcome of TBI, prior mouse models of TBI were incompatible with sleep recordings. In the current study, we modified the classical weight-drop mouse model to be compatible with a headset for recording electroencephalogram (EEG) and electromyogram, and to replicate effects of SWS modulation on TBI outcome measures. The resulting mild TBI mouse model shows cognitive impairment, EEG abnormalities, and DAI. Such DAI was reduced following treatment with sodium oxybate during the first 3 days after trauma, concomitant with increased slow-wave activity. Chemogenetic modulation of basal forebrain cholinergic neurons, on the other hand, did not reduce slow-wave activity. Overall, in the present study, we characterized an adapted weight-drop mouse TBI model for studying the relationship between sleep and TBI and provided additional evidence on involvement of sleep in neuronal recovery.

papers.title: Criterion-related validity, classification accuracy, and misclassification patterns of the International Fitness Scale in adolescents from a rural Mediterranean region of Spain: The EHDLA study.
papers.abstract: Self-reported fitness instruments provide a scalable surveillance solution when objective testing is impractical, yet the nature of perception-accuracy discordance in adolescents is not well understood. This study examined criterion-related validity, classification accuracy, convergent construct validity against the Spanish Perceived Physical Literacy Instrument (S-PPLI), and misclassification patterning of the International Fitness Scale (IFIS) in a community sample of adolescents from the Valle de Ricote (Region of Murcia, Spain). Cross-sectional data from 1017 Spanish adolescents (471 boys, 546 girls; median age 14 years) from the Eating Healthy and Daily Life Activities (EHDLA) study were analyzed. IFIS overall correlated with the Assessing the Levels of Physical Activity and Fitness (ALPHA-Fit) composite (Spearman rho [ρ] = 0.369; partial ρ = 0.377, p < 0.001), with flexibility showing the strongest domain-specific validity (Spearman ρ = 0.635; partial ρ = 0.592, p < 0.001). Using the full five-level IFIS score, the area under the curve (AUC) for identifying the lowest fitness tertile was 0.66 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.63-0.69). At the primary screening cut-off (IFIS ≤ 3), sensitivity was 0.68, specificity was 0.59, and negative predictive value was 0.80, while a stricter threshold (IFIS ≤ 2) increased specificity (0.94) at the cost of sensitivity (0.16). Convergent validity with S-PPLI was supported (partial ρ = 0.56, p < 0.001). Misclassification profiling identified 18.5% of participants as underestimators and 17.6% as overestimators; underestimation was associated with shorter sleep, while concordant-low membership was associated with higher body mass index (BMI), lower activity, and more sedentary time. In conclusion, IFIS showed weak-to-modest criterion-related validity and limited discriminative accuracy. Therefore, IFIS may serve as a low-burden adjunct to objective testing for population-level prioritization, but its performance relative to other brief instruments or low-burden measures, including BMI, remains untested. Discordance between perceived and objective fitness was common (36.1%) and co-occurred with lifestyle and adiposity characteristics, supporting consideration of perception-accuracy profiling in school-based and public health surveillance. Findings pertain to a single rural region and require replication in urban, regional, and socioeconomically diverse samples before broader generalization.
papers.journal: Journal of exercise science and fitness

papers.title: A Novel DHX9 Variant Was Identified in a Patient With Developmental Delay, Facial Dysmorphism and Seizure.
papers.abstract: The DHX9 gene encodes an RNA helicase belonging to the DExD/H-box family, which is highly expressed in the brain and nervous system. Pathogenic variants in the DHX9 gene are associated with neurodevelopmental disorder (NDD) and Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT). Both loss-of-function (LoF) and missense variants can cause NDD, whereas CMT is associated with specific missense variants. Patients with DHX9-related NDD typically present with intellectual disability, language and motor developmental delay, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). CMT patients primarily present with distal weakness, sensory deficits, variable muscle wasting, foot deformities and painful sensory neuropathy. Here, we report a female patient with severe DHX9-related NDD phenotypes, including global developmental delay, ASD, facial dysmorphism, epilepsy, microcephaly, abnormal brain MRI findings and clinodactyly of the fifth finger. She experienced her first febrile seizure at 1 year and 2 months of age. She developed frequent myoclonic seizures characterized by rapid nodding and upper body tremors lasting 3-10 s at the age of 3 years. Simultaneous electroencephalogram (EEG) revealed paroxysmal bursts of high- to very-high-amplitude sharp-slow waves, spike-slow waves and polyspike-wave complexes diffusely over bilateral leads. Clinical exome sequencing (CES) identified a likely de novo missense variant in the DHX9 gene in the patient (NM_001357.5, c.1540C>T, p.(His514Tyr)). Notably, this variant resides within the highly conserved DEIH motif (Motif II) of the helicase ATP-binding domain. This critical region plays an essential role in ATP hydrolysis and helicase function. Three-dimensional protein structure modelling suggested that the p.(His514Tyr) substitution may compromise local protein stability by altering hydrogen bond networks. Our study expands the genetic and phenotypic spectrum of DHX9 variant-associated disorders.

papers.title: Using the International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health Framework to Document Real-World Functional Outcomes in Inpatient and Outpatient General Rehabilitation.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND The International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF) provides a standardized framework for documenting rehabilitation outcomes beyond diagnosis-based reporting. This study aimed to assess the use of ICF-based profiles for describing real-world functional outcomes in inpatient and outpatient general rehabilitation in Poland. MATERIAL AND METHODS A retrospective secondary analysis was conducted using anonymized implementation-pilot data from 674 inpatient and 601 outpatient general rehabilitation patients. ICF qualifiers were recorded at baseline and at the end of rehabilitation for Body Functions, Activities and Participation, and Environmental Factors. RESULTS In Body Functions, significant reductions were observed in both profiles for energy and drive (b130), sleep (b134), emotional (b152), pain (b280), exercise tolerance (b455), urination (b620), joint mobility (b710), and muscle power (b730). In Activities and Participation, inpatient rehabilitation showed significant reductions across all analyzed codes, including daily routine (d230), body position (d410, d415), transferring (d420), walking (d450), self-care (d510-d550), looking after one's health (d570), interpersonal interactions (d710), and remunerative employment (d850). In the outpatient profile, significant changes were observed in most codes, including community mobility (d460), transportation (d470), housework (d640), and assisting others (d660), but not d240, d550, or d920. Environmental Factors were analyzed as facilitators and were stable or changed only minimally over time. CONCLUSIONS ICF-based profiles captured multidimensional functional changes in routine general rehabilitation, while Environmental Factors complemented outcome assessment by describing supportive contextual resources.
papers.journal: Medical science monitor : international medical journal of experimental and clinical research

papers.title: Development and EEG Assessment of a Virtual Reality Replica of a Prior Real Multisensory Environment Intervention.
papers.abstract: Multisensory environments (MSEs) are valuable therapeutic spaces for relaxation and stress relief, yet high costs and physical infrastructure limit accessibility. Immersive virtual reality MSEs (V-MSEs) offer a low-cost and scalable alternative to real MSEs (R-MSEs), but evidence is scarce. The aim of this study is an exploratory characterization of the electroencephalography (EEG) response to a V-MSE replica of a previous R-MSE intervention, using the original R-MSE data as a qualitative reference. After developing a V-MSE mirroring the original environment, 31 healthy participants underwent an adapted version of the protocol, and spectral and nonlinear features were computed from EEG recordings pre- and post-intervention. Analyses were performed within each environment, and comparisons between them remained qualitative. The alpha/beta ratio, negatively correlated with stress, was the only feature significantly increased in both conditions. In the V-MSE, frontal theta and the theta/beta ratio also increased significantly, whereas relative gamma power and Lempel-Ziv complexity decreased. Only in R-MSE, parieto-occipital alpha power rose significantly, whereas frontal delta power decreased. No feature changed significantly in opposite directions between settings. Evidence remains insufficient to establish V-MSEs as an alternative to R-MSEs, but this first EEG characterization of a V-MSE is encouraging enough to justify broader studies.

papers.title: The Effect of Telemedicine-Based APAP Management on 24-Hour Ambulatory Blood Pressure in Patients with Obstructive Sleep Apnea: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
papers.abstract: Telemedicine improves access to obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) care, but whether telemedicine-based auto-adjusting positive airway pressure (APAP) management is noninferior to in-person care for the 3-month change in 24-hour mean blood pressure (BP) remains uncertain. To determine whether comprehensive telemedicine-based APAP management is noninferior to standard in-person care in reducing 24-hour mean BP in patients with OSA. In this prospective, randomized non-inferiority trial, 344 participants with suspected OSA were randomized 1:1 to telemedicine-based (TM) or in-person (IP) management for 3 months. The primary outcome was the between-group difference in change in 24-hour mean BP. The prespecified non-inferiority margin was 1.5 mmHg. Secondary outcomes included APAP adherence, patient-centered outcomes and metabolic parameters. Of 344 randomized participants, 256 completed the 3-month follow-up (127 IP and 129 TM). The between-group difference (TM - IP) in the change in 24-hour mean BP was -0.59 mmHg (95% CI, -2.42 to 1.25) in the intention-to-treat analysis and -1.21 mmHg (95% CI, -3.24 to 0.81) in the completer analysis. Both upper confidence limits were below the prespecified 1.5-mmHg non-inferiority margin. No clear evidence of between-group differences was observed in APAP adherence, patient-reported outcomes, or metabolic measures. Telemedicine-based APAP management was noninferior to in-person management for the 3-month change in 24-hour mean BP, using a prespecified margin of 1.5 mmHg. These findings support telemedicine as a potential alternative delivery model for blood pressure management in patients with OSA.
papers.journal: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

papers.title: Home-Built environment as medicine for long-term cancer survivorship: a hard pill to prescribe.
papers.abstract: Cancer survivorship is increasingly recognized as a chronic, accelerated aging-related state of health, with long-term care occurring largely within the community and home-built environment (H-BE)-the human-made or modified structures of the dwelling. Lifelong environmental exposures-such as fine particulate matter, circadian-disrupting light, and toxic chemicals-can exacerbate post-treatment inflammaging, disrupt resolution of inflammation, and shape trajectories of long-term outcomes. Yet patient-level H-BE interventions targeting these modifiable, non-lifestyle risk factors remain an overlooked clinical domain in survivorship research, clinical guidelines, and care delivery. In this Commentary, we present an evidence-based, living framework that positions the H-BE as an emerging, prescribable target for mitigating late toxicities, symptom burden, and their physiological precursors in aging cancer survivors. The framework is structured across eight Emerging Frontline Domains, interdependent capability areas to guide next-generation survivorship trials in the practice of H-BE as medicine and advance clinical translation primary care-level H-BE screening and dual clinical-environmental risk stratification; referral pathways and follow-up structures with BE health expertise; real-world characterization of H-BE exposure scenarios; drug-environment interaction mapping; shared mechanistic and biomarker-informed domains capturing inflammatory burden, inflammaging, and capacity to resolve inflammation; implementation technologies enabling longitudinal remote monitoring; and decentralized, adaptive and personalized trial designs to support scalable outpatient delivery. H-BE as medicine addresses a critical gap for middle-aged and older cancer survivors-those most affected by treatment-driven inflammaging, multimorbidity, and prolonged home exposure-and offers a mechanistically robust, actionable roadmap to advance H-BE interventions from research through feasibility testing into survivorship clinical practice.
papers.journal: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
